subject: The Fed hiked, Canada held, fixed rates rose
bodyMarkdown:
The Fed published the minutes of its September meeting yesterday afternoon, and if you are renewing a mortgage in the next few months, that document is doing more to set your rate than anything the Bank of Canada has done all year.

## What the Fed actually argued about

Bloomberg reported on Wednesday that every official backed the quarter-point hike the Fed made on September 16, the one that took the federal funds target range to 3.75 to 4.00 per cent and was its first increase since 2023. The unanimity is the boring part. Reuters, reading the same minutes, found the committee split on what it had just done. Some treated the hike as precautionary. Others saw the start of meaningfully tighter policy, and several participants said they did not consider the current rate restrictive at all. Most thought another quarter point would likely be appropriate by year end. So the Fed agreed on one move and on almost nothing after it. Traders have taken the softer read, and Reuters notes they now expect a hold on October 28, with December 8 and 9 the meeting that counts.

## The gap is already in Canadian mortgage rates

Canada's policy rate is 2.25 per cent. The American midpoint is 3.875 per cent. That spread of about 160 **basis points**, each one a hundredth of a percentage point, is what pushes money out of the loonie, and the Bank of Canada's own daily exchange rates put the U.S. dollar at 1.4257 Canadian on Wednesday, up from 1.4243 on October 1. The sharper effect is on fixed mortgages, which lenders price off bond yields rather than off the policy rate. Canadian Mortgage Trends reported that the five-year Government of Canada yield topped 3.7 per cent on Monday, against roughly 2.6 per cent in February, and that CIBC and TD raised select three and five-year fixed rates on Tuesday. Ratehub's figures as of Wednesday had the lowest insured five-year fixed at 4.34 per cent and the lowest variable at 3.4 per cent.

## Why Ottawa probably will not follow

UBS, Manulife, Oxford Economics and Scotiabank all now expect the Bank to raise its rate on October 28. CIBC disagrees, writing that "the case for a parallel Canadian hike at this moment gets much weaker," and that Canada may wait until 2027. I lean toward CIBC, and the reason is jobs. Statistics Canada reported on September 4 that employment fell by about 42,000 in August, the employment rate slipped to 60.8 per cent, and unemployment held at 6.4 per cent, with youth unemployment at 12.9 per cent. The September survey lands tomorrow morning, and it is the first full month of data since U.S. Section 338 tariffs took effect on August 22. RBC Economics expects employment up 5,000 and the jobless rate unchanged. A central bank looking at that number does not hike into it just because Washington did.

## The takeaway

If you are renewing before spring, take the fixed rate you can get rather than waiting on the Bank of Canada, because the thing moving your fixed rate is a bond yield that has climbed a full percentage point since February and needs no rate decision to climb further. If you are sitting in a variable, the discount is real, but you are betting against four forecasters who have put their October call in writing. Read tomorrow's jobs report for the unemployment rate rather than the headline job count, since that is the line the Bank keeps pointing at. Then mark October 28, when the Bank announces at 9:45 a.m. and the Fed at 2 p.m., the one day this month you get both answers at once.
